title: Turning points of US history
description: Independence (1776), the Constitution (1787), the Civil War (1861 to 1865) and the end of slavery (1865), Pearl Harbor (1941) and the Moon landing (1969).

facts.text: The American Civil War (1861 to 1865) was fought between the United States and 11 Southern states that seceded and formed the Confederacy.
The 13th Amendment, ratified on December 6, 1865, abolished slavery in the United States.

title: The Dred Scott decision
description: In 1857 the Supreme Court ruled that Black Americans were not citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories.

facts.text: Dred Scott, an enslaved man, sued for his freedom because he had lived in a free state and a free territory.
On March 6, 1857, Chief Justice Roger Taney ruled that Black Americans, free or enslaved, were not US citizens and could not sue in federal court.
The Dred Scott ruling said Congress had no power to ban slavery in the western territories.

title: From Harpers Ferry to secession
description: John Brown's raid and Lincoln's election led seven Deep South states to secede, and their own declarations named slavery as the reason.

facts.text: In October 1859, John Brown led a party of 22 raiders to seize the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, hoping to spark a revolt of enslaved people.
US Marines under Robert E. Lee captured Brown, and Virginia hanged him for treason on December 2, 1859.
Many Northerners hailed John Brown as a martyr, while many white Southerners saw his raid as proof of a Northern plot against the South.
In November 1860, Republican Abraham Lincoln, who opposed slavery's spread into the western territories, won the presidency without carrying a single slave state.
Lincoln said he had no purpose to interfere with slavery in the states where it already existed.
South Carolina seceded on December 20, 1860, and in February 1861 seven seceded states formed the Confederate States of America, with Jefferson Davis as president.
Mississippi's 1861 declaration of secession stated: "Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery."
Several seceding states issued declarations of causes that named the defense of slavery as their reason for leaving the Union.

title: Fort Sumter starts the war
description: The Confederate attack on Fort Sumter in April 1861 began the war; Lincoln's call for troops pushed four more states out.

facts.text: On April 12, 1861, Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, and Major Robert Anderson's outnumbered, undersupplied garrison surrendered.
No one was killed in the bombardment of Fort Sumter itself.
On April 15, 1861, Lincoln called for 75,000 militia to put down the rebellion.
After Lincoln's call for troops, Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina and Tennessee seceded, bringing the Confederacy to 11 states.

title: The border states
description: Four slave states stayed in the Union; their people, resources and routes made keeping them vital, which made Lincoln cautious about emancipation.

facts.text: Four slave states, Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky and Missouri, stayed in the Union; they were called the border states.
The border states held large populations, farms and minerals, and key transportation routes; losing them would have badly weakened the Union.
In September 1861, Lincoln wrote: "I think to lose Kentucky is nearly the same as to lose the whole game."
Fear of pushing the loyal slave states toward the Confederacy made Lincoln cautious about freeing enslaved people early in the war.

title: Emancipation as a war measure
description: Lincoln framed emancipation as a war power to save the Union, issuing it after Antietam as a military necessity.

facts.text: In an August 22, 1862 letter to Horace Greeley, a New York editor, Lincoln wrote: "My paramount object in this struggle is to save the Union."
When Lincoln wrote to Greeley, a draft of an emancipation proclamation was already on his desk.
After the Union victory at Antietam, Lincoln issued a preliminary Emancipation Proclamation on September 22, 1862.
Lincoln issued the Proclamation as commander in chief, calling it "a fit and necessary war measure for suppressing said rebellion."

title: What the Emancipation Proclamation did
description: From January 1, 1863, enslaved people in rebelling areas were declared free, with exemptions for loyal areas, and Black men could join the Union forces.

facts.text: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect on January 1, 1863, declaring enslaved people in areas in rebellion "are, and henceforward shall be free."
The Proclamation applied only to areas in rebellion; it left slavery untouched in the loyal border states and in Confederate areas the Union already held.
After January 1, 1863, every advance of Union troops widened the area where enslaved people were legally free.
The Emancipation Proclamation announced that Black men would be accepted into the Union Army and Navy.

title: Self-emancipation
description: Enslaved people who escaped to Union lines, starting at Fort Monroe in 1861, forced the question of freedom; historians debate how to weigh their role and Lincoln's.

facts.text: In May 1861, Frank Baker, Shepard Mallory and James Townsend escaped slavery and rowed a small boat to Fort Monroe, a Union fort in Virginia.
General Benjamin Butler refused to return them, declaring people who fled to Union lines "contraband of war."
Within months, hundreds more enslaved people had fled to Fort Monroe.
On June 2, 1863, Harriet Tubman helped lead a Union raid up the Combahee River in South Carolina that freed more than 700 enslaved people.
Historian Ira Berlin argued that enslaved people were the prime movers of their own emancipation; James McPherson argued Lincoln's role was decisive.
Much recent scholarship shows self-emancipation working together with military emancipation and laws passed by Congress.

title: Black soldiers in the Union forces
description: About 179,000 Black men served in the Union Army, fighting at places like Fort Wagner despite unequal pay until 1864.

facts.text: About 179,000 Black men served in the Union Army, 10 percent of it, and about 19,000 more served in the Navy.
Black soldiers were first paid $10 a month minus $3 for clothing, while white privates got $13; Congress granted equal pay in June 1864.
In July 1863 the 54th Massachusetts led an assault on Fort Wagner, South Carolina; about 272 of its roughly 650 men were killed, wounded or captured.

title: Gettysburg and Vicksburg
description: In July 1863 the Union stopped Lee's invasion at Gettysburg and took Vicksburg, splitting the Confederacy along the Mississippi.

facts.text: The Battle of Gettysburg, fought in Pennsylvania from July 1 to 3, 1863, ended Robert E. Lee's second invasion of the North.
As many as 51,000 soldiers from both armies were killed, wounded, captured or missing at Gettysburg, the war's bloodiest battle.
On July 3, 1863, about 15,000 Confederates attacked the Union center in Pickett's Charge; the assault failed, and Lee retreated to Virginia.
Vicksburg surrendered on July 4, 1863, giving the Union control of the Mississippi River and splitting the Confederacy.

title: The Gettysburg Address
description: Lincoln's short speech of November 1863 tied the war to 1776's promise of equality and a "new birth of freedom."

facts.text: On November 19, 1863, Lincoln gave the Gettysburg Address at the dedication of a cemetery for Union soldiers killed in the battle.
The Gettysburg Address is roughly 270 words long.
The address opens "Four score and seven years ago," 87 years before 1863, pointing to 1776 and the proposition "that all men are created equal."
Lincoln closed by resolving that the nation "shall have a new birth of freedom" and that government "of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth."

title: Sherman's hard war
description: Sherman took Atlanta and marched to the sea in 1864, destroying railroads and supplies to break the South's ability to fight.

facts.text: Union general William T. Sherman captured Atlanta on September 2, 1864, a victory that helped Lincoln win reelection that November.
From November 15 to December 21, 1864, Sherman's army marched about 285 miles from Atlanta to Savannah, living off the land and destroying railroads and supplies.
Sherman aimed to wreck the Confederacy's ability to make war and to bring the war home to Southern civilians.

title: Drafts and riots on the home fronts
description: Both sides drafted soldiers, the rich could buy their way out, and anger boiled over in New York's draft riots and Richmond's bread riot.

facts.text: The Confederacy passed the first national draft in American history in April 1862.
The Union's Enrollment Act of March 3, 1863, let a drafted man hire a substitute or pay $300 to avoid service.
Critics called the conflict "a rich man's war but a poor man's fight."
In July 1863, New York City draft rioters attacked Black residents and burned the Colored Orphan Asylum; more than 100 people were killed.
On April 2, 1863, women in Richmond, the Confederate capital, many of them soldiers' wives, rioted over food prices, crying "Bread or blood!"
Dorothea Dix became superintendent of women nurses for the Union Army in 1861, and thousands of women served as nurses.

title: How the war ended
description: Lincoln called for peace without malice; Lee surrendered at Appomattox on April 9, 1865, after a war that killed 620,000 to 750,000.

facts.text: In his second inaugural address on March 4, 1865, Lincoln urged the nation on "with malice toward none, with charity for all."
In the same address, Lincoln said that slavery was "somehow the cause of the war."
Robert E. Lee surrendered his army to Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House, Virginia, on April 9, 1865.
Grant's terms let Confederate soldiers go home on parole, and those who owned horses or mules could keep them for farming.
About 620,000 soldiers died by the long-accepted count; a 2011 census-based study by J. David Hacker estimated about 750,000.

title: Lincoln's assassination
description: Booth killed Lincoln in April 1865, putting Andrew Johnson and his lenient terms for the South in charge of Reconstruction.

facts.text: John Wilkes Booth, a Confederate sympathizer, shot Lincoln at Ford's Theatre in Washington on April 14, 1865; Lincoln died the next morning.
Vice President Andrew Johnson, a Southerner who had opposed secession, was sworn in as president on April 15, 1865.
Johnson pardoned most white Southerners and let former Confederate states rebuild their governments with little federal oversight.
Many Republicans in Congress were outraged by Johnson's pardons, as Southern states sent former Confederate leaders to Congress.

title: The 13th and 14th Amendments
description: The 13th Amendment ended slavery (except as punishment for crime); the 14th made everyone born here a citizen with equal protection, undoing Dred Scott.

facts.text: The 13th Amendment bans slavery and involuntary servitude "except as a punishment for crime."
The 14th Amendment, ratified July 9, 1868, made "all persons born or naturalized in the United States" citizens.
The 14th Amendment bars states from denying any person "due process of law" or "the equal protection of the laws."
Congress wrote the 14th Amendment's citizenship clause to undo the Dred Scott decision.
Historian Eric Foner calls the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments a "second founding" because they remade the Constitution.

title: The 15th Amendment
description: The 15th Amendment (1870) barred race discrimination in voting but left out women, splitting the women's rights movement.

facts.text: The 15th Amendment, ratified February 3, 1870, bars denying the vote "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude."
Because the 15th Amendment did not cover women, Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony opposed it, while Lucy Stone and Frederick Douglass supported it.

title: What Reconstruction achieved
description: The Freedmen's Bureau built schools and Black men voted and won office, including the first Black senator and representative in 1870.

facts.text: Congress created the Freedmen's Bureau on March 3, 1865; it set up schools, oversaw labor contracts and helped freedpeople reunite with family.
Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first African American US senator in 1870.
Joseph Rainey of South Carolina, born enslaved, became the first African American in the US House on December 12, 1870.

title: How Reconstruction ended
description: Klan terror and massacres like Colfax attacked Black voters, and after the disputed 1876 election federal troops left the South in 1877.

facts.text: Confederate veterans founded the Ku Klux Klan in Pulaski, Tennessee, in 1865 or 1866; it used terror against Black Americans to undo Reconstruction.
On April 13, 1873, armed white men attacked Black defenders of the courthouse in Colfax, Louisiana; estimates of the Black dead run as high as about 150.
After the disputed 1876 election, Democrats accepted Republican Rutherford B. Hayes as president, and in 1877 he withdrew the last federal troops protecting Southern Republican governments.
Historian C. Vann Woodward (1951) argued a secret bargain settled the 1876 election; Allan Peskin (1973) questioned whether it was a true compromise.

title: Civil War and Reconstruction: freedom won, equality lost
description: Between 1865 and 1877 the nation ended slavery and wrote citizenship and voting rights into the Constitution, then withdrew the federal protection of those rights.

facts.text: Between 1865 and 1877, the US abolished slavery and wrote citizenship and voting rights into the Constitution, then withdrew federal troops from the South.
